title: How Well Do You Know the Gospels?
subtitle: Test your grip on the four accounts of Jesus' life.
about: Four writers, four vantage points, one life. Matthew wrote for a Jewish audience looking for their Messiah, Mark moved fast for an urgent Roman reader, Luke researched carefully as a doctor and historian, and John circled back decades later to tell what the other three had left out. Knowing the Gospels well means noticing what each one was written to show.

verses.text: but these are written, that ye may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God; and that believing ye may have life in his name.

it seemed good to me also, having traced the course of all things accurately from the first, to write unto thee in order, most excellent Theophilus; that thou mightest know the certainty concerning the things wherein thou wast instructed.

questions.text: How many Gospels are there in the New Testament?

options.explanation: Three would leave one of the writers out, and all four have their own book.
Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John each tell the story of Jesus in their own way.
There are only four Gospels. The book of Acts follows them, but it is not a Gospel.
Seven is a number that shows up a lot in the Bible, but there are just four Gospels.

questions.text: Which Gospel is the shortest and moves the fastest?

options.explanation: Matthew is long and full of Jesus' teaching, like the Sermon on the Mount.
Mark is the briefest Gospel and keeps the action moving, often using the word 'straightway.'
Luke is the longest Gospel and even opens by saying he set things in order carefully.
John is unique and reflective, but Mark is the shortest of the four.

questions.text: Which Gospel opens with the words, "In the beginning was the Word"?

options.explanation: Matthew opens with a genealogy tracing Jesus back to Abraham.
Mark opens with John the Baptist preparing the way, not with the Word.
John 1:1 (ASV) begins, "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God."
Luke opens with a note to a man named Theophilus, then moves to the birth stories.

questions.text: Who baptized Jesus in the Jordan River?

options.explanation: Peter was one of Jesus' disciples, called later in the story.
John baptized Jesus in the Jordan, and the Spirit came down like a dove (Matthew 3:13-17).
Andrew was Peter's brother and a follower of Jesus, not the one who baptized Him.
Elijah lived centuries earlier. Some thought John came in the spirit of Elijah, but it was John who baptized Jesus.

questions.text: How many disciples did Jesus choose as His apostles?

options.explanation: Seven men were later chosen to serve tables in Acts, but the apostles were more.
Ten leaves two of the apostles out of the count.
Jesus chose twelve apostles, a number that echoes the twelve tribes of Israel (Mark 3:14).
Jesus also sent out seventy others, but His inner circle of apostles was twelve.

questions.text: On which mountain did Jesus give the teaching that includes the Beatitudes?

options.explanation: Mount Sinai is where Moses received the Law, long before Jesus.
The Mount of Olives appears later, near Jesus' final days, but not for the Beatitudes.

options.text: A mountain, in what we call the Sermon on the Mount
options.explanation: Matthew 5:1-2 says Jesus went up a mountain and began to teach, giving the Beatitudes.
Mount Carmel is where Elijah faced the prophets of Baal in the Old Testament.

questions.text: Which Gospel is traditionally linked with a doctor and pays close attention to the poor and outsiders?

options.explanation: Luke is tied to a physician of that name (Colossians 4:14) and often highlights the lowly and the lost.
Mark is fast and action-driven, but it is Luke who is linked with a doctor.
Matthew was a tax collector and wrote with a Jewish audience in mind.
John focuses on who Jesus is, with long talks and seven signs.

questions.text: Who betrayed Jesus to the religious leaders?

options.explanation: Thomas doubted the resurrection at first, but he did not betray Jesus.
Judas handed Jesus over for thirty pieces of silver (Matthew 26:14-16).
Peter denied knowing Jesus three times, but Judas was the betrayer.
Bartholomew was one of the twelve, but he was not the betrayer.

questions.text: What did Peter do three times on the night Jesus was arrested?

options.explanation: That night was about fear, not healing. The healings came later in Acts.
Peter denied Jesus three times before the rooster crowed, just as Jesus had said (Luke 22:54-62).
Peter did fall asleep in the garden, but the thing he did three times was deny Jesus.
Peter walked on water earlier in Jesus' ministry, not on the night of the arrest.

questions.text: Who was the Roman governor who allowed Jesus to be crucified?

options.explanation: Herod the Great ruled at Jesus' birth and ordered the killing of the infants in Bethlehem.
Caesar Augustus called for the census around Jesus' birth, but he was far away in Rome.
Pilate questioned Jesus, washed his hands, and handed Him over to be crucified (Matthew 27:24-26).
Felix was a later governor who heard Paul's case in the book of Acts.

questions.text: What did the women find when they came to Jesus' tomb on the first day of the week?

options.text: The stone rolled away and the tomb empty
options.explanation: They found the stone rolled back and were told, "He is not here; for he is risen" (Matthew 28:6, ASV).
Guards had been posted, but by morning the stone was rolled away and the tomb was open.

options.text: Jesus still wrapped in the cloths
options.explanation: The grave cloths were left behind, but Jesus' body was gone. He had risen.

options.text: An empty garden with no tomb
options.explanation: The tomb was right there. What was missing was the body of Jesus.
